name: The ABC Model
lede: A thought isn't a fact. We'll look at one moment together — what happened, what you made of it, and what that led to.
why: Separating the event (A) from the belief about it (B) from what followed (C) makes visible something that usually happens too fast to notice. Naming the thinking pattern matters as much as naming the thought — most of us run the same two or three patterns, and spotting yours is where the loosening starts. This is the standard ABC cognitive model with the unhelpful-thinking-styles step used in CBT self-help; the wording here is our own.

steps.title: How this works
steps.body: Short prompts, one at a time. Where there's a blank box you'll find examples you can tap and edit — you never have to start from nothing. Skip anything that doesn't fit, and nothing saves until the end.

steps.help: Just the facts, like a camera would see it.
steps.placeholder: e.g. I opened my inbox on Sunday night and saw a message from my manager
examples: I saw a message from my manager and didn't open it
A friend didn't reply to my text all day
I made a mistake in front of other people
I woke up already dreading the day

steps.prompt: B — Belief: what went through your mind?
steps.help: Word for word if you can. You don't have to argue with it.
steps.placeholder: e.g. If I got this wrong, everything falls apart
examples: If I got this wrong, everything falls apart
They're annoyed with me and I've ruined it

steps.prompt: How much do you believe that thought right now?
Does that thought fit any of these patterns?
steps.help: Most of us run the same two or three. Spotting yours isn't self-criticism — it's the useful bit. Tap any that fit.
options: Catastrophising — jumping to the worst outcome
Mind reading — assuming I know what they think
All-or-nothing — total success or total failure
Should statements — I ought to be handling this
Emotional reasoning — it feels true, so it is
Filtering — only the bad part sticks

steps.prompt: C — Consequence: how did you feel, and what did you do?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Chest went tight, I closed the laptop and avoided it all evening
examples: Chest went tight and I avoided it all evening
I went quiet and stopped replying to people
I over-explained and apologised too much
I couldn't settle, kept checking my phone

steps.help: Pick whichever feels least forced. Skipping is fine.
options: What would I tell a friend in this exact situation?
What part of this can I actually control?
What would I think about this in a week?

steps.prompt: So — what's a slightly wider way to hold it?
steps.help: Not forced positivity. Just a little more room. Tap an example if you're stuck.
steps.placeholder: e.g. One message isn't the whole story; I can read it properly tomorrow
examples: One message isn't the whole story — I can read it properly tomorrow
I don't actually know what they're thinking yet
This is one moment, not the whole pattern
I'd tell a friend this was understandable, not a failure
The part I control is what I do next, not what already happened

steps.prompt: And now — how much do you believe the original thought?

nextSteps.label: Ground & Settle
nextSteps.because: That thought is still loud. Sometimes the body needs settling before the mind will follow — this takes about 90 seconds.

nextSteps.label: One Small Action
nextSteps.because: You've done the looking-at-it part. One small action is often what makes it stick.
